items.prompt: What is 'symmetric encryption'?
choices: Encryption where the same single key both encrypts and decrypts
Encryption that uses a different algorithm for encrypting versus decrypting
Encryption that only works on messages of a fixed, symmetric length
Encryption that requires two different people to each hold half a key
items.explanation: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both directions — encryption and decryption are the same secret, applied both ways.
items.reference:
Symmetric encryption
🔑 One shared key
⚡ Fast
Why: the shared key has to reach both parties somehow, which is the problem this unit centers on.

items.reference:
Symmetric encryption

items.prompt: What is 'asymmetric encryption'?
choices: Encryption using two mathematically related keys, where anything encrypted with one can only be decrypted with the other
Encryption that uses a different key for every single message sent
Encryption that only works between exactly two specific people
Encryption where the ciphertext is a different length than the plaintext
items.explanation: Asymmetric encryption relies on a mathematically related key pair — public and private — rather than one shared secret.
items.reference:
Asymmetric encryption
🔑🔒 Public/private key pair
🐢 Slower, but no shared secret needed
Why: it solves key distribution at the cost of speed.

items.prompt: According to L1, what does asymmetric encryption make possible that symmetric encryption doesn't?

Encrypting data faster than symmetric encryption ever could

Encrypting a message without needing any key at all
items.explanation: The unique capability L1 highlights is enabling secure communication with no prior secret exchange — exactly what solves the key distribution problem.

items.prompt: What is true of a 'public/private key pair'?
choices: The public key can be shared with anyone openly; the private key must never leave its owner's possession
Both keys must be kept equally secret at all times
The two keys are identical copies of each other
Only the private key can be shared; the public key must stay hidden
items.explanation: The defining asymmetry is that one key (public) is safe to expose while the other (private) must remain exclusively with its owner.
items.reference:
Public/private key pair
📢 Public: safe to expose
🔒 Private: never leaves the owner
Why: only the matching private key can decrypt what the public key encrypted.

items.prompt: Implement `xorEncryptDecrypt(bytes, keyByte)`, a simplified illustration of a symmetric cipher's core property: the same operation, run with the same key, both encrypts and decrypts. Given an array of byte values and a single key byte, return a new array where each byte has been XORed with `keyByte`. (This is a toy illustration of the symmetric round-trip property, not a real cryptographic algorithm — L3's actual encryption uses AES-256-GCM via Node's crypto module.)

tests.description: encrypting then decrypting with the same key recovers the original
tests.expr: (() => { const original = [72, 101, 108, 108, 111]; const encrypted = xorEncryptDecrypt(original, 42); const decrypted = xorEncryptDecrypt(encrypted, 42); return expect(decrypted).toEqual(original); })()

tests.description: the encrypted bytes differ from the original
tests.expr: (() => { const original = [72, 101, 108, 108, 111]; const encrypted = xorEncryptDecrypt(original, 42); return expect(JSON.stringify(encrypted) === JSON.stringify(original)).toBe(false); })()

tests.description: decrypting with the wrong key does not recover the original
tests.expr: (() => { const original = [72, 101, 108, 108, 111]; const encrypted = xorEncryptDecrypt(original, 42); const wrongDecrypt = xorEncryptDecrypt(encrypted, 99); return expect(JSON.stringify(wrongDecrypt) === JSON.stringify(original)).toBe(false); })()

items.explanation: XOR has the property that applying it twice with the same value returns the original — `(b ^ k) ^ k === b`. This illustrates, in miniature, the core symmetric-encryption property from L1: the same key (and here, the same operation) both encrypts and decrypts. It is not secure for real use — real symmetric encryption (like AES-256-GCM in L3) uses a much more complex transformation specifically to resist the kind of pattern analysis a simple XOR cipher is vulnerable to.
items.reference:
Symmetric round-trip
🔑 Same key, same key
🔄 Same operation both ways
Why: a toy illustration of why symmetric encryption needs one shared secret.

items.prompt: Implement `xorWithRepeatingKey(bytes, key)`, extending the previous idea to a multi-byte key: given an array of byte values and an array of key bytes, XOR each byte in `bytes` with the key byte at the corresponding position, cycling back to the start of `key` when it runs out. (Again, a simplified illustration of the round-trip property, not a real cipher — see L3's actual AES-256-GCM usage.)

tests.description: encrypting then decrypting with the same key recovers the original
tests.expr: (() => { const original = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]; const key = [5, 7]; const encrypted = xorWithRepeatingKey(original, key); const decrypted = xorWithRepeatingKey(encrypted, key); return expect(decrypted).toEqual(original); })()

tests.description: the key cycles back to the start for longer inputs
tests.expr: (() => { const original = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]; const key = [5, 7]; const encrypted = xorWithRepeatingKey(original, key); expect(encrypted[0]).toBe(original[0] ^ key[0]); return expect(encrypted[2]).toBe(original[2] ^ key[0]); })()

items.explanation: Using `i % key.length` cycles through the key bytes for inputs longer than the key itself, while preserving the same round-trip property as the single-byte version — applying the same repeating key twice recovers the original.
items.reference:
Symmetric round-trip
🔑 Same key, same key
🔄 Same operation both ways
Why: a toy illustration of why symmetric encryption needs one shared secret.
